edges.description: Circulating gonococci and their products localize to the synovium and tendon sheaths.
Circulating gonococci seed dermal vessels, producing the skin lesions of the triad.
Bacteremia produces the systemic febrile response.
Bacteremia produces rigors and chills.
The systemic bacteremic response drives peripheral leukocytosis.
The acute-phase response to bacteremia elevates C-reactive protein.
Hematogenous seeding of the endocardium produces rare endocarditis.
Hematogenous seeding of the meninges produces rare meningitis.
Synovial seeding produces migratory polyarthralgia.
Tendon-sheath seeding produces tenosynovitis.
Viable organisms proliferating in a joint establish a purulent intra-articular infection.
Intra-articular infection produces arthritis.
Purulent joint infection is a septic arthritis.
Sustained or delayed-treated purulent arthritis causes permanent joint damage.
Contiguous spread from an infected joint produces osteomyelitis of the adjacent bone.
Dermal seeding produces the dermatitis of the triad.
The characteristic lesions are pustular or vesiculopustular.
Small-vessel injury produces petechial and hemorrhagic lesions.
C5 blockade removes the membrane attack complex, reproducing the host susceptibility of terminal complement deficiency.

nodes.description: Congenital deficiency of a terminal complement component (C5-C9), or pharmacologic blockade of C5 by eculizumab, removes the membrane attack complex that is the principal bactericidal defence against Neisseria. A host lacking MAC can be disseminated even by strains that are not strongly serum-resistant, which is why terminal complement deficiency and C5 inhibitors are recognized DGI risk factors. The genes bound here are the terminal components C5-C9 named by the cited source; properdin (CFP) deficiency, an alternative-pathway defect also linked to neisserial infection, is not bound because no cited source here names it for DGI.

nodes.description: Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody that blocks C5 and prevents membrane attack complex formation, is an iatrogenic phenocopy of terminal complement deficiency and markedly raises the risk of disseminated, often blood-culture positive, gonococcal infection. Patients on eculizumab should be counselled about this risk and screened for sexually transmitted infections; if antibiotic prophylaxis is used, gonococcal resistance trends should guide the choice.
